articles.title: Build a capture
articles.summary: Generate a pcap, then find the files.
articles.body:
## Steps

1. Under Starting point, pick one button: Clean baseline, Security, Performance, Crypto posture, OT / ICS day or Incident replay. Clean baseline adds no scenarios and puts every moved scenario back to its own time. Each button shows an Undo link for ten seconds. See [[undo-a-change]].
2. Under Choose scenarios, change the selection if you want. Use the category rail, the search box and the family chips to find scenarios. Press Details on a scenario to open its card, then Add to capture or Remove from capture. The strip above, The capture day, shows where each scenario falls in the 16 hours.
3. In the right panel, set Company name and Industry. Both are optional. A blank company name becomes Example. See [[company-and-industry]].
4. Set Capture date. It starts as today. Pin a date to make two runs comparable.
5. Set Size with the slider or Quick sample, Standard or Full day. The slider starts at the Default size in Settings, or at the size your last session had. The line beside it estimates file size and packet count, and the progress bar during a build reads against the same estimate. See [[baseline-and-scale]].
6. Open More options to change the Output folder (default `~/OpenGenerator-Captures`) or untick the certificate and threat collection exports, both ticked by default. Advanced: addressing and OT changes the user and server networks or adds an OT network. See [[addressing-and-networks]].
7. Press Generate capture. Stop cancels and discards the partial capture. A build that fails removes its partial capture too. In both cases an earlier build in the folder is put back. If you build again with different settings, the earlier build is kept, not overwritten, and the result says where. See [[earlier-builds]]. When the build ends, the app moves to Captures.

## Find your files

In Captures, the file table lists the pcap first, such as `example-all-in-one.pcap`. Press Reveal in folder to open it. See [[generation-report]] and [[captures-and-files]].

## If something goes wrong

- Generate capture is disabled. Hover over it. The message names the missing dependency or empty field. Settings has a Re-check button.
- The build shows Failed. Try a smaller size.
- Captures says No capture yet. No build has finished in this session. Check the output folder named in Earlier captures, or build one from Compose.

articles.title: Import and validate a pcap
articles.summary: Turn your own pcap into a recipe and add it to a build.
articles.body:
## Before you start

- Switch on Lab tools in Settings. See [[settings-and-lab-switch]].
- The file must be a pcap or pcapng of 1 GiB or less.

## Steps

1. Click Lab in the top bar, then Import pcap. The step strip shows Choose a file, Profile, Save recipe and Add as scenario.
2. Pick a file. The list under the strip shows up to five captures from your output folder, each with a Choose button. For any other file, type its full path in Or type a path and press Tab or click away.
3. Wait for Reading the capture. Four tiles appear: Flows, Protocols, Duration and Size. If the file cannot be read, a red message says why and the strip returns to Choose a file.
4. Click Open profile report. A new tab shows what the app found and which protocols it can and cannot recreate. See [[lab-import-pcap]].
5. Click Save recipe. The app writes `<capture name>-recipe.json` into your output folder and shows the path and flow count. Add as custom scenario and Reveal in folder appear.
6. Click Add as custom scenario. The Recipes tab opens and the recipe joins Custom recipes in the next build. See [[lab-recipes]].
7. Go back to Compose and click Generate capture. The build includes one CUSTOM scenario for each recipe in the list. See [[build-a-capture]].
8. When the build finishes, return to Lab, Import pcap. Under Check the rebuild, type the new capture's path in Capture built from the recipe, then click Compare with the original. A report opens in a new tab.

## What the result means

The new capture uses the app's own hosts, addresses and users, not those in your file. Protocols the app has no builder for are listed as not recreated and left out. See [[addressing-and-networks]].

## If something goes wrong

- Enter a file path first, or click the field and pick a suggestion: the path box was empty.
- The file is not a pcap or pcapng: choose a different file.
- The CUSTOM scenario is missing from the build: open Lab, Recipes and check the list.
- Compare with the original asks for a path: fill in both the original path in Or type a path and the new capture path.

articles.title: Replay a capture onto a sensor
articles.summary: Play a capture onto a network interface.
articles.body:
Replay needs tcpreplay, which you install separately.

## Before you start

- Have a capture. See [[build-a-capture]].
- Know which network card is cabled to the sensor's monitoring port or SPAN or TAP feed.
- Expect a macOS administrator prompt. The password goes to macOS, not to this app.

## Steps

1. Click Replay in the top bar, or Replay this capture in Captures after a build. Use for replay on an earlier capture does the same for that file.
2. Check the dependency chips under Replay on the wire. If tcpreplay is missing, a red message gives the install command. Install it, then reload the page.
3. Capture file holds your last build. Type another path to replay a different file.
4. Choose the card in Replay interface. The app marks one as recommended.
5. Choose a Speed. Original timing x multiplier is the default: 1 is real time, 2 is twice as fast, 0.5 is half speed. Top speed, Fixed packets/sec and Fixed Mbps ignore the capture's timing.
6. Set Loops to the number of times to play the capture. 1 plays it once.
7. Leave Open a monitor window ticked to get a Terminal window showing tcpreplay's output. Control-C there stops the replay without a password.
8. Tick I understand - start the replay. Start replay stays greyed out until you do.
9. Click Start replay and approve the macOS prompt. The progress panel shows Played as a percentage, send rate and elapsed time. The top bar chip changes to Replaying.
10. When it ends the title reads Replay complete. Click Stop replay to end it early; the title then reads Stopped, noting the capture was partly played.

- The replay runs as a separate process. Reloading the page, opening a second tab or restarting the app does not stop it. Quitting the app on purpose does.
- A sensor with the matching threat collection raises threat matches during replay. See [[lab-sensor-pushes]].

## If something goes wrong

- Start replay stays disabled: tick the acknowledgement, install tcpreplay, or wait for a running replay to finish.
- It says a replay is already in progress. Only one replay runs at a time. Wait for it to end or press Stop replay.
- It says tcpreplay will not be run as root. Replay runs it as administrator, so from 6.0 the app does so only for a `tcpreplay` whose file and folder are both owned by root and not writable by anyone else. One in your home folder is refused, and the message gives a one-time command that puts a root-owned copy in `/usr/local/bin`, where the app looks. On macOS every library the tool loads must also sit in a root-owned folder that others cannot write. Homebrew's `tcpreplay` loads `libdnet` from a folder you own, so it is refused even as a root-owned copy, and the message names the library. Install `tcpreplay` with MacPorts (`sudo port install tcpreplay`) or use a statically linked build, or run the app as root. Replay without administrator rights is not affected.
- The interface and tool checks on the Replay page are reused for a few seconds, so a fix you made a moment ago can take a few seconds to show. Start still re-checks before it sends.
- Could not start replay: read the message under the form. The app re-checks the file and interface before it asks for a password.

articles.title: VLAN tagging
articles.summary: An opt-in setting that puts an 802.1Q tag on every frame. Off by default.
articles.body:
A capture is untagged by default. VLAN tagging is an option for sensors that expect frames from a trunk or a mirror port. It changes nothing unless you ask for it, and the default day and its packet count stay as they were.

In Compose, open Network options and turn on VLAN tagging. Choose one VLAN per subnet or one fixed ID, and add an outer tag if you want QinQ. On the command line it is `--vlan` and `--vlan-qinq`.

## Choices

- `--vlan` or `--vlan subnet`: each flow gets one VLAN ID, taken from the segment where the capture sees it. The ID is the third number of that subnet, so 10.10.20.0/24 becomes 20. A third number of 0 becomes 1. Both directions of a flow carry the same ID.
- `--vlan 120`: every frame gets the one ID you give, 1 to 4094.
- `--vlan-qinq` or `--vlan-qinq 300`: adds an outer 802.1ad service tag over the 802.1Q tag. The outer ID defaults to 100. It implies `--vlan`.

## What to expect

- The 4-byte tag is added before the frame is padded to the 60-byte minimum. A tagged frame is therefore not always exactly 4 bytes longer than the same frame untagged. A short frame can absorb the tag in its padding.
- Byte counts in the manifest and the report are bytes as written to the file, tags included.
- The setting is part of the build parameters. A tagged and an untagged build of the same scenarios never count as the same build, so one does not replace the other. See [[earlier-builds]].
- The manifest records the setting, how many frames were tagged and how many tag bytes that added.
- The Zeek-style TLS and HTTP logs still read tagged captures. The flow truth file and the flow export do not: they read untagged IPv4 only, so on a tagged capture every frame is counted as unflowed and they hold no flows. See [[build-exports]].

## Not covered

With tunnels on as well, a tunneled frame between two hosts on the same subnet gets the default VLAN ID. See [[tunnel-carriers]].

The per-subnet choice reads IPv4 and ARP addresses. IPv6 frames from the dual-stack option are tagged too: the segment comes from the sending host, or from the subnet part of a private IPv6 address. A link-local frame from an unknown sender gets the default segment. See [[ipv6-dual-stack]].

articles.title: Build exports
articles.summary: Opt-in files beside the pcap: a flow truth file, Zeek-style logs and a pcapng copy.
articles.body:
Exports are extra files written beside the pcap after a build. All are off by default and cost nothing unless asked for. In Compose, open Exports and turn on the ones you want. Each shows a rough size. On the command line use `--exports` once for each: `truth`, `ssl`, `http` and `pcapng`. Flow export (`ipfix`, `netflow9`) is command line and API only. See [[flow-export-ipfix]].

Any export also writes a small tag file, `<name>.tags`, with one byte per packet naming the scenario that made it.

## Zeek-style, not Zeek

The logs use Zeek's column names, types and header block, filled by this app's own rules. They have not been compared with a real Zeek run, so treat a field as approximate unless it is listed as exact below.

## The files

- **`<name>-truth.jsonl`.** One line per flow, with the scenario that produced it, whether it is normal-day traffic, packet and byte counts, TCP flags and first and last packet numbers. The packet numbers match the pcap. A flow ends after 300 s idle for TCP (Zeek's published value), 60 s for UDP and 30 s for ICMP. The UDP and ICMP values are placeholders and not measured against any sensor. A SYN after a FIN or RST starts a new flow. The file reads untagged IPv4 only. IPv6 and VLAN-tagged frames are counted as unflowed.
- **`<name>-ssl.log` and `<name>-x509.log`.** TLS handshakes and the certificates seen in the clear. A real TLS 1.3 handshake is encrypted, so those rows carry no certificate chain. The `cert_dates` column is not a Zeek column. It says whether the leaf was valid at the flow time.
- **`<name>-http.log`.** One row per plain HTTP request. Sizes are bytes on the wire, not decoded sizes. HTTPS content is not read.
- **`<name>.pcapng`.** The pcap converted, with the same packets and times. `--pcapng-comments` adds each packet's scenario as a comment. `--pcapng-embed-keys` embeds the TLS key log so one file decrypts in Wireshark. Embedding is off by default.

## What is exact and what is approximate

The Zeek-style logs follow IPv4 TCP only, so the dual-stack IPv6 traffic does not appear in them. Exact: packet and flow counts, times, packet numbers, the scenario tags and the pcapng contents. Approximate: connection states, the history string, services named by port, and everything that Zeek derives from payload.

## Reproducibility

The exports are a fixed function of the pcap and its tag file, so the same pcap gives the same export. Two rebuilds are not byte-identical: certificates and some payload bytes are random.

An export that fails is recorded in the manifest and the capture is kept. The tag file stops at 256 different tags. Past that the truth export is skipped.

articles.title: Cut a slice out of a capture
articles.summary: Copy one scenario's time window or packets into a smaller pcap, from the Captures page or the command line.
articles.body:
A full day at 1x takes about 16 hours to replay. A slice holds one scenario's traffic so you can replay it in less time. A slice copies packets exactly as they are and never changes the original files.

## Steps

1. Open Captures and expand Cut a slice of one scenario.
2. Choose a capture. The list holds classic pcap files from the output folder, and never a slice of a slice. A capture needs its build manifest beside it.
3. Choose a scenario. Only scenarios that put packets in the file are listed.
4. Choose the kind. A takes every packet in the scenario's time window, plus the padding each side. B takes the scenario's own packets and baseline packets near them. C takes only the scenario's packets.
5. Set the padding in seconds (default 300). For B and C, set Background to None, Inside the padded spans, or The whole capture's background.
6. Read the preview line, then press Cut slice.
7. Find `<name>.slice.<scenario>.<kind>.pcap` and its `.json` sidecar beside the capture. The result shows the packets kept and the original packet numbers of each kept span. Use for replay opens the Replay page with the slice chosen.

The sidecar names the source pcap's hash, the spans used and the original packet numbers. The command line does the same from a source copy: `python3 tools/slice_pcap.py <name>.pcap --scenario <scenario> --kind A`, with `--ctx` and `--baseline`.

## Which kind to use

- **A** is the faithful one. It is the same traffic the sensor sees in the full day, including other scenarios running at the same time. It needs no tag file.
- **B and C** are experiments. The sensor sees a different traffic mix than in the full capture, so an alert may appear or vanish. They need the build's tag file, which any export switched on in Compose writes. The slice file says which kind it is.

## Caveats

- Timestamps are copied unchanged. A replay shifts packets by their gaps, so a live sensor stamps its own time. A sensor that reads the file reads its original dates. Moving dates by days with a rebase makes certificate and ticket times inside the payloads disagree with the packet times.
- Replay at 1x. Capping gaps with `--maxsleep` shortens the run but breaks the rhythm that beacon and brute-force detections watch for.
- A resumed replay is not one continuous 1x run. See [[replay-record-and-resume]].
- The slicer refuses a manifest whose hash does not match its content.

## If something goes wrong

- It says the tag file is missing for B or C. Rebuild with an export, or use kind A.
- It says the manifest was edited. Use the manifest the build wrote.
- It says the slicer is not part of this build of the app. The slicer is a file in the source tree's `tools` folder. The packaged apps that have been checked do not include it, so cut from a source copy.

articles.title: The replay record and resume
articles.summary: Each replay leaves a small record beside the capture. A stopped run can pick up where it left off.
articles.body:
Each replay that starts traffic writes one small file beside the capture, `<name>.replay-<id>.json`. It lets a later result on the sensor be tied to what was sent.

## What the record holds

- The file replayed, by name, size and sha256. A full capture takes its hash from its manifest. A slice names its source capture.
- The speed, loop count, packet range, any rebase and any pause cap.
- When it started and stopped, how many packets went out, and whether it finished, was stopped or failed.
- The kind of interface, such as wired or file. Never its name.
- A label you chose for the sensor and a note.
- Whether the run was a continuous 1x run.

It never holds a sensor address, key, token or provider setting, a file path, or the text of an error. The label cannot be an address. A record that cannot be written does not fail the replay.

## Resume

A run that was stopped or failed can continue. The app finds the next packet that was not sent and starts a few packets earlier, so nothing is lost at the join. The overlap is 500 packets unless you set another, 0 to 100,000.

- Only a single pass (loop 1) can be resumed.
- A finished run, or a run whose position is unknown, cannot.
- The file must be the one that run replayed. A pcapng file cannot be resumed.
- A resume sets its own packet range, so it cannot also take one.

A resumed run is not a continuous 1x run. Its record says so and names the run it continued.

## Where this is available

Records and resume belong to the person at the app. An agent has no verb for them.

On the Replay page, Replay records for this capture lists each record for the capture in the file field, oldest first. View shows its facts and the full JSON. A run that can resume shows Resume from packet N. That button only fills the form: it sets Resume an earlier run under More replay options and reminds you that a resumed run is not continuous. Press Start replay to go ahead. A record marked as changed since cannot be resumed from the list. The same options hold a packet range, a longest-pause cap, a sensor label and a note.

articles.title: Scenario expectations
articles.summary: A data file that says what each scenario's traffic does and what a sensor could raise.
articles.body:
`scenario_expectations.json` describes every scenario, all 81 of them, in plain data. There is no screen for it yet, and nothing in the app scores a sensor against it.

## What each entry has

- A summary of what the traffic does.
- The roles involved: attacker, victim and infrastructure. They are inventory role names, never addresses.
- The ATT&CK techniques the traffic shows, with a tactic and a note, and industrial-control techniques where they apply.
- How much the result depends on the baseline.
- Expected detections. Each has a class from a fixed vocabulary of 49, a strength and a status.

## Strength and status

Strength is expected, plausible or informational. There is no stronger level, because that needs evidence from a live sensor. Every entry starts at status authored. The later statuses (reviewed, run-observed, run-confirmed, disputed) are for a person to set when evidence exists.

## The validator

From a source copy, `python3 tools/check_expectations.py` lists every problem and exits 1 if there are any. It checks that every scenario has an entry and none is stale, that technique ids exist and fit their tactic, that classes, strengths and statuses come from the fixed lists, that timing hints fit each scenario's window, and that no name or path breaks the neutrality list. The test suite runs it, so a new scenario without an entry fails the gate.

articles.title: Replay on Linux
articles.summary: How replay picks an interface and gets raw-socket rights on Linux, and the one-time setcap fix.
articles.body:
Replay needs `tcpreplay`, which is installed separately. On Linux the app names the command for your distribution: `sudo apt install tcpreplay` on Debian and Ubuntu, `sudo dnf install tcpreplay` on Fedora, `sudo dnf install epel-release && sudo dnf install tcpreplay` on RHEL-family systems, and the matching command for openSUSE, Arch and Alpine. The app never runs it for you.

## Choosing an interface

Interfaces are ranked. Loopback, virtual interfaces (containers, VMs, bridges, tunnels) and the interface that carries this computer's default route are listed last and carry a warning. Replaying on the default route can put traffic on a production network. They stay selectable. The suggestion is the fastest wired link that is up and not warned about.

## How it gets permission

Sending raw packets needs rights. The app tries these in order and says which it chose:

1. Already running as root.
2. `tcpreplay` has the `cap_net_raw` capability. No prompt.
3. Passwordless `sudo` for that exact `tcpreplay` binary. The app checks with `sudo -n` and never prompts.
4. `pkexec`, when a desktop session is present. A system dialog asks for an administrator password, and the password goes to that dialog, never to the app. Stop cannot end a replay started this way before it finishes.
5. None of these. The message gives the fix.

## The one-time fix

As an administrator, run `sudo setcap cap_net_raw+ep $(command -v tcpreplay)`. Run it again after `tcpreplay` is upgraded. This avoids the password dialog and keeps Stop working.

## Status

This is new in 6.0. It was written and tested with simulated system answers, and has not yet been confirmed on a Linux machine. For the app itself, see [[install-on-linux]].

articles.title: Add dual-stack IPv6 traffic
articles.summary: An opt-in slice of IPv6 traffic added on top of the IPv4 day. Off by default; the default capture is unchanged.
articles.body:
The default capture is IPv4. The dual-stack option adds a slice of IPv6 traffic on top of it, for sensors that should see both. It is off by default. A default build and its packet count do not change.

Use `--ipv6` or `--ipv6 0.4` on the command line. In the API, send `network_options` with `ipv6` set to `true`, a share, or an object such as `{"share": 0.4, "chatter": false}`. The Compose page has no control for it.

## What it adds

- Neighbour discovery, Router Advertisements, multicast listener queries and reports, and DHCPv6, as background chatter. `"chatter": false` leaves these out and keeps only the flows.
- DNS, HTTPS and SMB flows over IPv6 from a share of the workstations. The share is a number above 0 and at most 1. The default is 0.25.
- Servers and gateways are always dual-stack. A workstation is dual-stack when a hash of its name falls under the share, so the same name is chosen every time.

## Addresses

Internal hosts get a private (ULA) address built from the company identity, the subnet and the host's own MAC. External hosts get an address in 2001:db8::/32, the documentation range. Addresses are derived, never drawn at random, so they are stable.

## What stays the same

Everything in the IPv6 slice is scheduled after the day and the scenarios, and carries its own `v6:` tags. It uses private random streams. Remove those frames and the rest of the capture has the same packet count, protocol mix, 5-tuples and times as a build without the option. The manifest records the option and a block for it, with packets and bytes per tag.

## Limits

- The IPv6 traffic is a slice, not a second copy of the day. Scenarios run over IPv4 unless you pick the IPv6 variants. See [[ipv6-scenarios]].
- The flow truth file, the flow export and the Zeek-style logs read IPv4 only. IPv6 frames are counted as unflowed in the first two and absent from the logs.
- With VLAN tagging on, IPv6 frames are tagged too. See [[vlan-tagging]].
- It was checked in the tests with independent IPv6 checks and, where available, Wireshark's command-line dissector. It has not been compared with a real dual-stack network or run against a sensor.

articles.title: IPv6 scenario variants
articles.summary: A campaign option that runs actions over IPv6, plus two IPv6 link-local attack scenarios.
articles.body:
Two additions put attack traffic on IPv6: a campaign option and two scenarios.

## Campaign option ip_family

A campaign has an option `ip_family` with three values:

- `v4`, the default. A campaign without the option is the campaign it always was.
- `v6`. Every action runs over IPv6.
- `dual`. Actions alternate: the first over IPv4, the second over IPv6, and so on in order.

Set it in the campaign file or the API. The Campaign Builder page has no control for it. Each action in the campaign summary records its family and, for IPv6, the addresses the capture carries. Actions run on private random streams, so the rest of the day does not move. IPv6 indicators in a feed are still carried but not placed in the capture.

## Two scenarios

Both are ordinary entries in the scenario list, in the NDR group. Pick them like any scenario. They do not need the dual-stack option.

- **IPv6 rogue RA and DHCPv6 takeover** (11:00 to 11:30). A workstation sends Router Advertisements, answers victims' DHCPv6 requests with its own address as the DNS server, serves a proxy-discovery file over IPv6 and collects NTLM from the fetch. It then reuses that identity against a file server over IPv4. This follows the public description of the mitm6 technique. The relay leg is SMB with the victim's account name, not an LDAP relay.
- **IPv6 neighbour-discovery flood** (11:40 to 12:10). A workstation floods the segment with Router Advertisements from random source addresses, each with a new prefix, then solicits addresses nobody holds, so the gateway retries each three times. It is filed under Impact. Some taxonomies call it discovery abuse.

Both have confidence medium in the scenario data. See [[scenario-expectations]].

## What was checked

The tests check that the default is unchanged, that the output is deterministic and that the shared random streams end where they started. They run the IPv6 checker and, where available, Wireshark's command-line dissector. No sensor was run against these scenarios, so what a sensor raises is expected, not observed.

articles.title: Flow export: IPFIX and NetFlow v9
articles.summary: Opt-in exports that write flow records as exporter packets plus a CSV. Collector acceptance is not verified.
articles.body:
Two more exports write flow records the way a router or switch would send them. They are off by default. Use `--exports ipfix` or `--exports netflow9` once for each. In the API, put the names in `exports`. Compose has no control for them yet.

## The files

- `<name>-ipfix.pcap` and `<name>-ipfix.csv`: IPFIX (RFC 7011), to UDP port 4739.
- `<name>-netflow9.pcap` and `<name>-netflow9.csv`: NetFlow v9 (RFC 3954), to UDP port 2055.

The pcap holds UDP datagrams from a synthetic exporter to a synthetic collector, both in 192.0.2.0/24, the documentation range. Each packet is stamped with the latest flow end time in its message, so the file replays in capture order. The CSV holds the same records. Both are listed in the manifest with their hashes, and `earlier-builds` moves them with their capture.

## The records

- One record per direction that carried packets, originator first. Both directions share the flow's one start and one end.
- Fields: addresses, ports, protocol, TCP flags, packets, octets, start and end times, ingress and egress interface, the VLAN ID when a record has one, and the scenario tag. For ICMP, the destination port field carries type times 256 plus code.
- Interface numbers, addresses, the observation domain and the tag element are synthetic values. The tag is enterprise element 1 of number 32473, the documentation number, so it is not a registered field. NetFlow v9 has no tag, so it is in the CSV only.
- Templates go out first, when first needed, and every 20 messages or 600 seconds of export time.

## Limits

- A flow is exported once, after it ends. There is no active-timeout splitting.
- Not implemented: bidirectional records, sampling, options templates, next hop, AS numbers, application ids.
- The flow table reads untagged IPv4 only. With VLAN tagging or the IPv6 option, those frames produce no records. See [[vlan-tagging]].
- The records are held in memory before writing, roughly 100 MB per million records. That figure is an estimate, not measured at full scale.
- It was decoded in the tests with Wireshark's command-line dissector and an independent decoder. No real collector has accepted these files. Acceptance by a collector is not verified.

The output is a fixed function of the pcap and its tag file. Two rebuilds are not byte-identical, as for the other exports.

articles.title: Where keys are stored
articles.summary: API keys and the agent token go to the macOS Keychain, the Linux desktop keyring, or a private file.
articles.body:
A key you choose to keep, and the agent token, go to one store. The app picks it when it starts, so the choice does not depend on what you click.

## The three stores

- **macOS Keychain.** Used on macOS. It behaves as it did before 6.0.
- **Desktop keyring on Linux.** Used when the `secret-tool` command is found in a system folder and a keyring answers a quick test. A locked keyring that waits for a prompt counts as not answering.
- **A private file.** Used on Linux when neither of the above works. It is `keystore.json` in the settings folder, mode 0600, in plain text. The app refuses to read it if another user owns it or others can read it, and tells you to run `chmod 600`.

The store in use and the reason are reported by the key status route, so a page can show whether keys are in a keyring or a file. A key never goes on a command line: it travels on the standard input of the helper.

## Things to know

- `secret-tool` is found only in fixed system folders, never through your PATH, because the secret passes through it. On Debian and Ubuntu it comes with `libsecret-tools`. A locked or missing keyring falls back to the file.
- The agent token lives in the same store. An older token kept in a separate token file is no longer read. Create a new token if an assistant stops being accepted after an update. See [[what-is-the-agent-api]].
- The settings folder is created private to you (mode 0700). A folder you chose with `OG_SETTINGS_DIR` is left as you made it.
- A plain file is weaker than a keyring: anything running as you can read it. Use a keyring if you can.

## Status

The three stores are tested with simulated system answers and a real private file. The keyring path has not been run against a live desktop keyring on a Linux machine. See [[replay-on-linux]] for the other Linux status notes.

articles.title: Install the Linux app
articles.summary: Check, unpack and run the Linux tarball, and add a launcher entry.
articles.body:
The Linux build is a tarball that holds the app and its own Python. It needs no root and writes nothing next to itself. The name is `apophis-<version>-linux-<arch>.tar.gz`, with `x86_64` or `aarch64`, and a `SHA256SUMS` file comes with it.

## Steps

1. Put the tarball and `SHA256SUMS` in one folder.
2. Run `sha256sum -c --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS` there. It must say OK for the tarball. If it does not, fetch it again.
3. Unpack it with `tar -xzf apophis-<version>-linux-<arch>.tar.gz`.
4. Run `apophis` inside the new folder, `apophis-<version>-linux-<arch>/`. The launcher starts the local server, prints its address and opens your browser. Closing the tab or pressing Ctrl-C stops it.
5. For a menu entry, run `./apophis --install-desktop` in that folder. It adds a launcher and icon for you under `~/.local/share` that point at this copy.

Other launcher options are `--no-browser`, which only prints the address, and `--version`. With no display it prints the address and does not look for a browser.

## Where things go

- Settings: `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/opengenerator`, or `~/.config/opengenerator`.
- The launcher's log: `$XDG_STATE_HOME/apophis/server.log`, or `~/.local/state/apophis`.
- Captures: the folder named in the app's page.

## Requirements

- It was built on AlmaLinux 9, so it needs glibc 2.34 or newer. RHEL 9 and Ubuntu 22.04 and anything newer qualify.
- Replay needs `tcpreplay` and raw-socket rights. See [[replay-on-linux]].
- Keys go to the desktop keyring or a private file. See [[where-keys-are-stored]].

## Status and limits

- The build recipe runs in containers and was checked by building the pinned baseline inside the bundle, on Ubuntu 22.04 and AlmaLinux 9, for x86_64. An aarch64 module list exists. Whether an aarch64 bundle has been run is not confirmed here.
- It has not been tried on every desktop. Packages for it are in [[linux-packages]].
- A tarball copy can update itself in the app. See [[update-on-linux]] for what is and is not verified.
- The slice picker does not work in this bundle, because the slicer is not included. See [[slice-a-capture]].

articles.title: Linux packages: deb, rpm, AppImage and Docker
articles.summary: The Linux app also comes as a .deb, an .rpm, an AppImage and a Docker recipe. What each needs, and what is unverified.
articles.body:
Besides the tarball, each Linux release has packages for both x86_64 and aarch64. One `SHA256SUMS` covers every Linux file in the release, both architectures. Download the files you want and `SHA256SUMS` into one folder, then run `sha256sum -c --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS`. Each file you have must say OK.

## The files

- `apophis_<version>_<amd64|arm64>.deb`: install with `sudo apt install ./<file>`. It depends on a minimum glibc and recommends `tcpreplay`, which apt installs by default.
- `apophis-<version>-<release>.<arch>.rpm`: install with `sudo dnf install ./<file>`. It recommends `tcpreplay`, but `tcpreplay` is in EPEL, so a stock RHEL-family system skips it. See [[replay-on-linux]].
- `apophis-<version>-<arch>.AppImage`: make it executable and run it. Where FUSE is missing, run it with `--appimage-extract-and-run`.

The deb and rpm put the app in `/usr/lib/apophis`, with `apophis` in `/usr/bin`, a menu entry and an icon. Every installed file is owned by root and none is writable by group or others. Settings and captures stay in your own home folder.

## Docker

`Dockerfile.app` builds an image from the .deb in Ubuntu 22.04 and runs as an unprivileged user. It is a recipe, not a published image. Build it with the `.deb` file named in a build argument, then run `docker run --rm --network host apophis`.

- The server listens on 127.0.0.1 only. The interface works only with `--network host`, on a Linux host. A published port (`-p`) cannot reach it.
- Replay does not work in the container. `tcpreplay` is left out on purpose. Make captures in the container and replay them from the host.
- Captures and settings live in the container user's home folder. Mount a volume there to keep them.

## Unverified

- The packages are unsigned. The in-app updater has its own signed manifest, which is separate. See [[update-on-linux]]. The checksums show a file arrived intact, not who made it.
- On the build host, the x86_64 AppImage runtime was not started under emulation. Its contents were unpacked and the baseline was run from them.
- RHEL 9 itself was not tried. AlmaLinux 9, a rebuild of it, stood in.
- Docker was not run on a real x86_64 host.
- The package checks are scripted. They were not rerun for this note.

articles.title: Update the app on Linux
articles.summary: How the in-app update works for a tarball or AppImage copy, why a deb or rpm copy refuses, and what is unverified.
articles.body:
On Linux the update dialog works as on macOS for patches. A newer full release is installed by the app only for a copy that you own and can write to: the tarball or the AppImage. A copy installed with a package manager is refused. See [[updates]] for the dialog.

## What the app checks

The release carries a signed manifest for your architecture (`og-app-<version>-linux-<arch>.json` and `.sig`). The app checks, in order, and changes nothing if any step fails:

1. The signature on the manifest.
2. The sha256 of the download against the signed manifest.
3. For a tarball, the sha256 of every unpacked file against the signed list. The new copy must also report the version the manifest names.

Then it swaps the new copy in and restarts. The old copy is kept in `app-previous` in the settings folder. An AppImage restarts through its own file path. The app never asks for a password and never escalates.

## Which copies can update

- **Tarball or AppImage in a folder you can write to:** yes.
- **Installed with apt, dnf or zypper (under `/usr/lib/apophis`):** no. The dialog says it was installed by your package manager and cannot update itself. Update it with the package manager, or install the newer release. See [[linux-packages]].
- **A folder you cannot write to:** no. The dialog tells you to download the newer release.

## For maintainers

`og-proof-linux` in `packaging/linux` runs the update against an unpacked tarball on a real Linux machine, with a throwaway signing key. It checks that a bad signature, a tampered manifest, a tampered download, a wrong per-file hash and a package-managed copy are all refused with nothing changed, then that an honest update applies and the baseline pin holds after it.

## Unverified

- The proof drives the updater from the source tree against a frozen 5.5 bundle, and its "new" bundle is the old one re-versioned. It shows the swap works, not that 6.0 code runs after it. The AppImage is swapped, not started.
- No real RHEL 9, and no x86_64 AppImage under emulation, was tried.

articles.title: Carry a scenario in a GRE, VXLAN or 6in4 tunnel
articles.summary: An opt-in setting that wraps chosen scenarios in a tunnel, for sensors that must decode one. Off by default.
articles.body:
Some sensors see traffic inside a tunnel. The tunnel option wraps the frames of the scenarios you name in GRE, VXLAN or 6in4. It is off by default, and a default build and its packet count do not change.

On the command line, repeat `--tunnel CARRIER:SCENARIO[,SCENARIO]`, for example `--tunnel gre:ndr-data-exfil`. `*` means every scenario and `normal-day` means the baseline. In the API, send `network_options` with `tunnels` as a list of `{"carrier", "scenarios", "mtu"}` objects. The Compose page has no control for it. A misspelled scenario name is an error, not a plain build.

## The carriers

- `gre`: IP protocol 47. It carries IPv4 and IPv6 packets. ARP and other non-IP frames pass through unwrapped.
- `vxlan`: UDP port 4789 with a network ID derived from the rule. It carries the whole Ethernet frame, ARP included.
- `6in4`: IP protocol 41. It carries IPv6 packets only. IPv4 and ARP frames pass through.

A scenario rides one tunnel. Each rule gets a pair of tunnel endpoints in 172.16.x.1 and 172.17.x.1, derived from the rule. The outer frame keeps the inner frame's MAC addresses. The manifest records `network.tunnels`: per rule, the frames wrapped, frames written, how many were fragmented, bytes added and frames passed through.

## Size and fragmenting

The outer packet never sets the Don't Fragment bit. A packet longer than the rule's `mtu` is split into IPv4 fragments, so one inner frame can become several. The default is 1500, and the range is 576 to 9000. A larger `mtu` leaves frames whole. A wrapped build therefore has more frames than the same build without it.

## What stays the same

The wrapper draws no random numbers. The inner frames are the same as in a build without the option, and every other scenario is untouched.

## Checking it

`check_rfc791.py` and `check_ipv6.py` take `--decap gre,vxlan,6in4`. They check the tunnel headers and then the packets inside.

## Limits

- With VLAN tagging also on, a tunneled frame between two hosts on the same subnet gets the default VLAN ID, not its subnet's. See [[vlan-tagging]].
- The flow files read untagged IPv4 TCP, UDP and ICMP. By those rules a GRE or 6in4 outer packet is not a flow and is counted as unflowed, and a VXLAN outer packet is one UDP flow. The inner frames are not read. This follows the flow-table rules and has not been run on a tunneled capture. See [[build-exports]].
- No tunneled capture has been replayed at a standard 1500-byte MTU, and none has been run against a sensor.

articles.title: Build a campaign
articles.summary: Turn threat indicators into attack traffic.
articles.body:
Nothing is sent to any real host. The builder only writes packets to a file.

## Steps

1. Open Campaigns. The Campaign builder shows four steps: Type, Indicators, Build and Save & run. On Type, pick Build from indicators and press Choose indicators. The other choices are Open a saved campaign (Open the library) and Start from scratch (Start empty).
2. On Indicators, either press Fetch next to a feed under Public feeds, or open Paste or load a file, paste text or press Load file, then press Add pasted indicators. Indicators per fetch sets how many to ask for. Some feeds need an API key, typed in the box beside the feed.
3. Review the table. Each row has a card, a type and a role. See [[indicator-cards]]. Use the Role, Type and Text filters to narrow it. The Dropped fold lists what was removed, such as private addresses and duplicates.
4. Under Compile a campaign, type a Campaign name. Choose the Compromised host, Lateral movement target, Beacons per C2, Start time, Speed and Beacon look (malware family). Tick the Stages to include, or choose a Goal or a template. See [[start-from-a-goal-or-template]]. Pick the Address mode. Mapped is the default and moves indicator addresses into a benchmark range, so the capture holds no real third-party address.
5. Press Compile campaign. When it succeeds, the builder reports how many stages it drafted and opens the Build step.
6. On Build, read the stages and actions. You can add a stage, move, duplicate or delete stages and actions, and change each action's settings. An estimate appears once the campaign is valid. Fix anything listed under Problems with the campaign.
7. On Save & run, Check shows whether the campaign is valid. Name and save has Save to library and Download JSON.
8. Under Run it, tick Use this campaign in the next capture.
9. Go to Compose and press Generate capture. The capture uses the Compose settings for size, company, networks and scenarios, and adds the campaign on top.
10. In Captures, the result card has campaign results: what ran, packets per action, the indicators as they appear in the capture and the files written. Open the campaign diagram opens a printable page. See [[generation-report]].

## Real addresses

Run it also offers Real addresses. Type `REAL` to confirm. The file then holds the indicators' own public addresses, and replaying it on a routed network can reach real hosts, so use an isolated lab only. See [[addressing-and-networks]].

## If something goes wrong

- Compile campaign asks for a selection. Select at least one indicator.
- Feeds show an error. A feed may need a key, or the network may be down. Paste a list or load a file instead.
- Many indicators show unknown. Add a role word such as `c2` or `scanner` to the line in your file and add it again.
- You leave the page with unsaved changes in the campaign editor. The browser asks first, in its own words. Save to library or Download JSON before you go.
- A campaign is armed that you did not arm. A session saves whether one is armed, but a restored choice is dropped when you first open or load a campaign.
- The campaign is not added. The Run it panel says it has problems. Open Check and fix them.

articles.title: Build a campaign from a threat report
articles.summary: Paste an advisory or article and see what traffic it would make.
articles.body:
Use this when you have a security advisory or news article and want its addresses and hosts as test traffic. Nothing is sent to any host named in the report. The builder only writes packets to a file.

## Steps

1. Open Campaigns. On Type, pick Build from indicators and press Choose indicators.
2. On Indicators, open Paste or load a file. Paste the report text and press Add pasted indicators.
3. Read the status line. If it says the text reads as a report, only addresses and defanged hosts were taken. See [[report-pasting-rules]].
4. Check the table. Each row has a badge, "on the wire" or "no traffic". Hover it to see why. If a Role looks wrong, change it.
5. Press Preview traffic in a row to see the actions, protocols and hosts that indicator would send. Press it again to close it.
6. Read the plan above Compile campaign. It lists the stages this selection will build.
7. Compile, review, save and generate as in [[build-a-campaign]].

## If something goes wrong

- Few indicators came in. Reports often hold links, file names and hashes. These are not taken from prose. Paste a plain list, or fetch a feed.
- A row says no traffic. It has no role, or it is a kind that never sends traffic on its own. Set a role such as `c2` or `scanner`.
- The addresses in the capture are not the ones in the report. That is the default Mapped mode. See [[addressing-and-networks]].

articles.title: Build a campaign from a CVE
articles.summary: Turn a known-exploited vulnerability into an inert attempt against its product.
articles.body:
Use this to test whether a sensor notices an attempt against a product with a known flaw. The capture holds the shape of the attempt and no exploit content.

## Steps

1. Open Campaigns, pick Build from indicators and press Choose indicators.
2. Under Public feeds, press Fetch next to CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities. To find CVEs on exposed hosts instead, use Shodan with your own key. See [[campaign-feeds]].
3. Only CVEs that name a network-facing product are listed. The rest are in Dropped, with a reason.
4. Read a card. It shows the CISA description and the required action. Press Preview traffic to see the Exploit-attempt probe it would send.
5. Under Compile a campaign, tick Initial access in Stages. The Goal named Reconnaissance and initial access ticks it for you.
6. Press Compile campaign, then continue as in [[build-a-campaign]].

## What to expect

- The probe asks for an endpoint typical of the product, posts a harmless form, and the server refuses. See [[cve-profiles-and-exploit-probe]].
- A sensor that looks for exploit content will not fire on it. A "missed" result tells you something about the sensor, not about the tool.

## If something goes wrong

- The CVE is missing. It was dropped because its product is not network-facing, such as a browser or office program.
- The row says no traffic. Check that Initial access is ticked.

articles.title: Start from a goal or a template
articles.summary: Build a campaign from an objective, with no feed and no network.
articles.body:
Use this when you know what you want to test but have no indicator list. The templates use documentation addresses and example domains, so nothing is fetched.

## Steps

1. Open Campaigns, pick Build from indicators and press Choose indicators.
2. Under Compile a campaign, open Start from a template and choose one. It fills the indicator list, the campaign name and the goal.
3. Or leave the list as it is and choose a Goal. A goal sets only the Stages and Beacons per C2. You can still change both.
4. Check the plan above Compile campaign.
5. Press Compile campaign, then continue as in [[build-a-campaign]].

## Goals

- Balanced intrusion
- Lateral movement
- Credential theft
- Data theft
- Ransomware
- Command-and-control beaconing
- Reconnaissance and initial access

Hover a template to read what it does. The five are Ransomware precursor, Credential theft chain, Slow data theft, Web-facing product compromise and Beacon-only test.

## If something goes wrong

- A goal changed my stages. That is its job. Tick or untick Stages afterwards.
- The list shows not available. The templates did not load.

articles.title: Export indicators to a spreadsheet or MISP
articles.summary: Get a CSV or a MISP event from a campaign build.
articles.body:
Use this to share a campaign's indicators with a ticket, a spreadsheet or a MISP server.

## Steps

1. Build a capture with a campaign. See [[build-a-campaign]].
2. Open Captures and find the result card for that build.
3. In the campaign results, open the list of files. Besides Campaign JSON, STIX indicator bundle, ATT&CK Navigator layer, Report and Report (web page), it now lists Indicators (CSV) and MISP event.
4. Open the file, or find it beside the pcap. See [[captures-and-files]].
5. To bring a MISP event back, use Paste or load a file in the builder and load it.

## What each file holds

- **Indicators (CSV).** Every indicator, the address it has in the capture, and whether it is on the wire. Cells that start with `=`, `+`, `-` or `@` are quoted, so a spreadsheet does not run them.
- **MISP event.** The indicators that are on the wire. It imports into a MISP server, or back into this builder.
- **STIX indicator bundle.** Only the indicators that appear on the wire, as they appear.

## If something goes wrong

- A file is missing. Only a build with a campaign writes them.
- An address differs from your list. Mapped mode moved it. See [[addressing-and-networks]].

articles.title: Add your own campaign action
articles.summary: Describe a web or text conversation in a JSON file and get a new action.
articles.body:
Use this to add a web request pattern or a plain-text conversation without writing Python. Other protocols still need a Python action.

## Steps

1. Make a folder for your specs. Set the environment variable `OPENGENERATOR_ACTION_SPECS` to its path before you start the app.
2. Add a JSON file. Start from the bundled example, `admin_panel_probe`.
3. For web traffic, give a `token`, `title`, `tactic`, `techniques` and `summary`. Then set `direction`, `port`, `tls` and the list of `requests`. Each request has a `method`, a `path`, a `status` and a `reply`.
4. For a text conversation such as SMTP, FTP or IRC, add `"kind": "tcp"`. Use an optional `banner` the server sends first, then `exchanges` of `send` and `reply`. Only the `\r` and `\n` escapes are allowed, and there is no TLS.
5. To have the compiler place the action itself, add `"for_role"` with a role such as `scanner` or `c2`. It then adds the action for up to three indicators of that role. The stage must be ticked.
6. Start the app. In Build, add the action from the editor like any other.

## Safety rules

Every field is checked. Bodies and replies are short printable ASCII, so a spec cannot carry a payload.

## If something goes wrong

- The action is missing. A spec that fails its checks is skipped. If you run from source, the errors are in `spec_actions.LOAD_ERRORS`.
- It is not in the compiled campaign. Without `for_role` you add it by hand.

articles.title: Import pcap (Lab)
articles.summary: Profile a pcap and save a recipe from it.
articles.body:
The tab shows only when Lab tools are on. See [[settings-and-lab-switch]].

The tool reads a pcap or pcapng and builds a profile: protocol and byte mix, hosts and roles, conversations, ports, timing, TLS and DNS names. From the profile it writes a recipe.

## What you give it and what you get

- Input: a pcap or pcapng, up to 1 GiB. Choose one of the five most recent captures in your output folder (an earlier build that a newer one displaced carries a Kept tag), or type a path.
- Open profile report: a report in a new tab naming the protocols the app can recreate and those it cannot.
- Save recipe: writes `<capture name>-recipe.json` into your output folder, then offers Add as custom scenario and Reveal in folder.
- Compare with the original: takes a capture built from the recipe and lists which of the original's protocols came back.

- Payload contents are never stored in the recipe.
- The rebuild uses the app's simulated hosts and addresses, so addresses from your file do not appear. See [[addressing-and-networks]].
- Protocols the app has no builder for are reported as not recreated and left out.

Full steps: [[import-and-validate-a-pcap]]. Saved recipes: [[lab-recipes]].

articles.title: Recipes (Lab)
articles.summary: The recipes the next build uses.
articles.body:
The tab shows only when Lab tools are on. See [[settings-and-lab-switch]].

A recipe is a JSON description of a scenario. The tool keeps a list of recipe files, and each one adds a CUSTOM scenario when you build in Compose.

## What you give it and what you get

- Input: type a path in Recipe file, or click the field and pick a recipe found in your output folder. Click Add recipe, or press Enter. A red message under the field reports a problem with the file.
- Output: the list under Custom recipes in the next build. Each row shows the path and a Remove button.

## When to use it

Use it after you save a recipe from [[lab-import-pcap]], or when you have a recipe file from someone else.

- Remove takes a recipe out of the list. It does not delete the file.
- A recipe that names protocols the app cannot build still adds the scenario. The unsupported flows are skipped and reported.

Full steps: [[import-and-validate-a-pcap]].

articles.title: Sensor pushes
articles.summary: Send a threat collection or replace decryption keys.
articles.body:
Turn on Lab tools in Settings to see this page ([[settings-and-lab-switch]]).

Sensor pushes sends material from a build to a monitoring appliance over its REST API. One panel is safe to repeat. The other deletes data on the target.

## Push the threat collection

A capture exports a file of the external indicators it used: command-and-control, exfiltration and malware-delivery hosts. Loading it into an appliance lets the appliance match those hosts when you replay the capture.

The push replaces only the collection the tool owns, named ExampleThreatCollection.

You give it:

- Appliance address
- API key
- Threat collection file
- Upload to: A sensor (standalone) or A console. A console syncs indicators to its connected sensors.
- Generate detections on an indicator match, on by default. With it off, matching hosts are tagged but no detection is raised.

Check appliance is read-only. It confirms the address and key, and says whether a previous collection will be replaced. Push threat collection runs the upload. The panel then shows counts for indicators in the file, imported, replaced and detections, plus a log.

## Danger zone: push certificates

This panel is marked Destructive. Push certificates deletes every SSL decryption key already on the sensor, then uploads the certificates for the current capture. Deleted keys cannot be recovered.

You give it a sensor address, an API key, a certificates folder, and a protocol and port. The protocol is HTTP, SMTP or LDAP, and the port defaults to 443. A key with no protocol mapping decrypts nothing.

Check sensor is read-only. It reports how many existing keys would be deleted. Push certificates stays disabled until the address, key and a valid port are filled in. Clicking it opens Replace all decryption keys?, where you press and hold Hold to delete and replace for 1.5 seconds.

- Run the certificate push only against a laboratory sensor.
- Appliances present a self-signed certificate. The connection is encrypted, but the app does not verify who answers, so confirm the address. The Check sensor and push reports show the sensor's certificate SHA-256, so you can notice a change.
- Sensor calls ignore proxy settings in your environment, so the key is never sent through a proxy.
- The API key is held in memory only and is forgotten when you close the page.

articles.title: Capability modules
articles.summary: Load, unload and test optional add-ons.
articles.body:
A capability module is an add-on you load and unload while the app runs.

It is under Lab, so turn on Lab tools in Settings first. See [[settings-and-lab-switch]]. A module can add a scenario to the list in [[scenarios-and-categories]].

## What you see

A line at the top counts what the app has built in: scenarios, diagrams, encoders, exporters and providers. Each module is a card with its name, kind, version and description. A loaded module shows loaded.

- Example marks a reference sample.
- 3rd-party marks a module added after install.
- Test runs the module's self-test and reports PASS or FAIL. It is enabled only while the module is loaded.
- Auto-load on startup keeps the module loaded after a restart.
- Test all loaded reports how many loaded modules passed.

## Effects on a capture

Scenario and encoder modules change the packets of a capture. While one is loaded, a note beside Generate says so; unload it to return to the baseline. demo_encoder and demo_scenario, both examples, change a capture. See [[baseline-and-scale]].

Loading a scenario module updates the scenario grid.

Modules run with the app's own access to your computer. Only add modules you trust.

articles.title: Settings and the Lab switch
articles.summary: Lab switch, appearance, defaults and API keys.
articles.body:
Settings is the slider icon in the top bar.

## Lab tools

Lab tools is off at first. Turn it on and a Lab tab appears, holding Import pcap, Recipes, Sensor pushes and Modules. Turn it off and Lab disappears; if you were on it, the app returns you to Compose. The choice is remembered in this browser.

See [[lab-import-pcap]], [[lab-recipes]], [[lab-sensor-pushes]] and [[lab-modules]].

## Appearance

Palette offers Slate Blue (the default), Forge, Teal, Sage and Clay. Theme is Dark, Light or System.

## Defaults

- Output folder is where captures are written. See [[captures-and-files]].
- Default size is Quick sample, Standard or Full day. It sets the size on a fresh start, when no session size is saved. A size restored from your last session or a loaded session wins over it until you change Default size here, which resets Compose's size at once.

## Sessions, Checks and API keys

See [[sessions]] for Sessions. Checks lists the dependency checks, with a Re-check button. API keys has a Forget stored keys button.

articles.title: Sessions
articles.summary: Saved form choices.
articles.body:
A session is the state of the form: company, industry, networks, size, ticked scenarios, timing moves, OT options, recipes, whether a campaign is armed for the next capture, and replay settings.

## The last session

The app saves your choices a moment after you change them. At the next start it restores them and shows Restored your last session, with a Start fresh button.

To turn this off, use Settings, Sessions, Restore my last session on start. The size you last chose comes back too. Settings under Defaults take priority over a restored session, except the Default size: that applies only when there is no saved size (a first start, or after Start fresh), and changing it in Settings sets the size at once. A campaign itself is not part of a session. Whether one is armed for the next capture is saved, but a restored armed choice is dropped when you first open or load a campaign, so a campaign is never armed by surprise.

## Named sessions

Under Settings, Sessions, type a name (up to 80 characters) in Save current state as and click Save. The session appears in a list with two buttons.

- Load puts that session's values back into the form.
- Delete removes it.

Loading a session, Start fresh, Select all, Clear selection, the starting-point buttons and Reset all each show an Undo link for ten seconds (Ctrl+Z or Cmd+Z does the same). Undo puts the form back as it was before that one action.

## Changed from default

Settings, Sessions lists what differs from a fresh start: ticked scenarios, timing moves, size, company, industry, recipes and an armed campaign.

## Export and import a setup

Export setup saves the same state as a named session to a file, apophis-setup.json. Import setup reads one back. The file is checked first: a file that is not a setup, or is from a newer version, is refused with a message and nothing changes, and values out of range (size, minutes moved) are brought back into range. An import can be undone like any other change.

## What is never saved

API keys, passwords, tokens and acknowledgement ticks are never stored. Lab tools, the palette and theme, and the output folder default are kept separately. See [[settings-and-lab-switch]].

articles.title: Updates
articles.summary: Small patches, whole-app updates and what the dialog says.
articles.body:
The download-arrow icon in the top bar, labelled Check for updates, opens a dialog.

## You are up to date

The dialog says You are up to date and names your version.

## A patch is available

A patch is a version whose last number is above zero, such as 5.5.1 after 5.5.0. It is a small update for the same major and minor version. The dialog shows the new version, your version and the release notes. Installing restarts the app, so finish any capture in progress first.

Click Install and restart, or Later.

On a 5.5.0 app, update straight to 5.5.3. Patches 5.5.1 and 5.5.2 cannot start on 5.5.0: the update installs, fails to start and is rolled back to 5.5.0 with your settings untouched. 5.5.3 fixes this. An app already rolled back needs nothing else.

## A newer version is available

From 5.5.0 on, Update can replace the whole app with the newest full release, from any older version. The dialog says Installing replaces the app and restarts it. Click Install and restart.

- The app downloads the new one, checks it, and swaps it in. It restarts by itself, and the page reloads when it is back.
- Your old app is kept in `app-previous` in the settings folder. Each new update replaces that copy.
- After the swap, check again. A patch for the new version may be waiting, so it can take two clicks.

## When the app cannot replace itself

The app cannot swap itself if it runs from a temporary location or from a folder it cannot write to. The dialog says The update was not installed, and one of these:

- Move the app to your Applications folder, open it from there, then update.
- The folder holding the app is not writable. Move the app to your Applications folder and update from there.

Nothing is changed.

## Linux

See [[update-on-linux]]. Checking again within a minute shows the earlier result.

## Versions before 5.5.0

An older app cannot update itself to a new full release. Its dialog offers Open releases page. Download the app once, then updating works from there.

## Other messages

- An update is already installing. Only one update runs at a time. Wait for it to finish.
- The new version did not start. Open the app again from Applications: it starts the version you had, and nothing is lost. Your settings, keys and captures are untouched. The dialog shows this after waiting a minute for the app to come back.
- A copy that runs from source says to update it with git pull.
- Could not check for updates. Try again in a moment.

articles.title: The normal day and the Size setting
articles.summary: The 16-hour day and the Size setting.
articles.body:
Every capture contains a normal business day for the simulated company, 16 hours long, from 05:00 to 21:00 on the capture date. With no scenarios selected, the button reads Generate baseline day.

## The Size setting

Drag the slider or press a preset. The number beside the slider is a multiplier from 0.001 to 1.

- Quick sample (0.02): builds in seconds.
- Standard (0.1): about 1.4 million packets of background plus the scenarios.
- Full day (1): about 10 million packets and 7 GB.

Smaller sizes keep the same mix of protocols.

## Size estimate

Next to the slider, an estimate such as "~0.9 GB · ~1.4M packets" covers the normal day plus each selected scenario. An armed campaign is added as a fixed amount. The note under the presets gives a build time, based on about 30,000 packets a second. The progress bar while a build runs is read against this same packet estimate, so the two agree.

## What changes with Size

The background day always grows with Size. Each scenario card has a chip, Fixed size or Grows with size. A growing scenario puts in less traffic at a small Size, so a volume-based detection can miss it.

With the OT network on, the polling interval is the biggest control on capture size.

articles.title: Company name and industry
articles.summary: Who the simulated organization is.
articles.body:
## Company name

Type up to 40 characters. A blank field becomes Example. The name sets:

- the Active Directory and DNS domain
- the host name prefix
- the Root CA
- the organization name that appears on the wire

With the default name, the domain is `corp.example.local` and host names start with `EXL-`. File names follow the name: `example-all-in-one.pcap`, or `acme-all-in-one.pcap` for Acme.

## Industry

Choose Logistics (the default), Manufacturing, Technology, Education, Healthcare, Finance, Retail, Energy or Government. It combines with the name, so Example and Logistics gives Example Logistics.

Choosing Energy adds two OT protocol options for electric utilities: synchrophasor (IEEE C37.118) and inter-control-centre data exchange (MMS over TCP 102).

Name and industry do not change the host count or traffic volume. Networks are set separately: [[addressing-and-networks]].

articles.title: Addressing and networks
articles.summary: User, server and OT networks.
articles.body:
You can change the simulated company's network addresses to fit your lab.

## Where to find the settings

In Compose, open More options, then Advanced: addressing and OT. The first two fields are User network (class C) and Server network (class C), with example values such as `10.10.10.0/24` and `10.10.20.0/24`.

## User and server networks

The user network holds 127 hosts: workstations, phones, access points, printers and boards. The server network holds 16: domain controllers, file, SQL and web servers, the phone system and the sensor.

Both must be /24 networks, and they must differ. Every host keeps its own last number when you change a network.

External addresses never change, including the threat-intelligence indicators used by security scenarios.

## OT network

Tick Add an OT network (class C) and type one /24 for the lowest control levels. The app adds two more /24 networks for site operations and the industrial DMZ. OT is off by default, and OT scenarios do nothing until you turn it on.

Diagrams and capture filters use the networks you set, not the defaults.

Classify those subnets in your monitoring platform before relying on OT results. Otherwise the OT devices land in an external or unknown zone.

articles.title: The generation report
articles.summary: Packets by protocol for your last build.
articles.body:
The generation report shows what a build wrote to the capture.

## How to open it

After a build, open More options in Compose and press View generation report, or press Generation report in the Next row in Captures. It opens in a new browser tab. Before your first build, the Compose button is disabled and Captures has no report button.

## What the report shows

Six numbers: Packets, Capture size, Protocols, Most packets, Scale and Scenarios. Below are a bar chart of packets by protocol and a table with each protocol's packet count and percentage, largest first.

## How the counts are made

Every frame is classified as it is written, so the counts are exact. Tunnelled traffic counts as its outer protocol.

## The CSV copy

The same table is written beside the capture as a file ending in `-generation-report.csv`, with the columns `protocol`, `packets` and `percent`.

## Other reports

Open report in the Earlier captures list opens a profile of that capture file. See [[import-and-validate-a-pcap]].

articles.title: Captures and the files a build writes
articles.summary: What a build writes and where it goes.
articles.body:
## Where files go

A build writes to the Output folder, set in Compose under More options or in Settings. The two stay in sync. The default is `~/OpenGenerator-Captures`.

## What a build writes

- The capture, named `example-all-in-one.pcap` by default.
- A TLS key log ending in `-tls-keys.log`, in the format Wireshark reads.
- A `certs` folder with a certificate and key for each simulated server, plus the issuing CA. Written when Export server certs + keys is ticked.
- A threat collection as `.stix.json` and `.csv` files, listing only the indicators your scenarios put on the wire. Written when Export threat collection is ticked.
- A build manifest ending in `.manifest.json`, recording the scenarios placed and the packets each produced.
- A generation report CSV. See [[generation-report]].

## When a build ends

The app switches to Captures. Packets by scenario lists each scenario with its packets, its size and whether it grows with the Size setting.

Stop discards the partial capture and key log. A failed build removes its partial capture, then shows the error and the end of the log.

## Earlier builds

A build never overwrites a different earlier build. If the output folder already holds a build with other settings, its files move to `earlier-builds/<UTC time>-<name>/` inside the folder. A rebuild with the same settings replaces the files, so you keep one set. The result panel says "Earlier build kept in" and the folder. See [[earlier-builds]].

## Earlier captures

Below the result, captures in your output folder are listed newest first, with Open report, Use for replay and Remove. Use for replay opens Replay with that file filled in.

Remove moves the capture and its related files to a holding folder; it does not delete them. A Removed list appears with a Restore button for each item.

A kept earlier build has a Kept tag. Its buttons, and Restore for a removed one, work on that build's own folder, not on the current capture.

articles.title: Undo a change
articles.summary: A ten-second Undo link after the actions that change many choices at once.
articles.body:
Some actions change many choices at once. After each of these, a message appears at the top right with an Undo button.

- a starting-point button (Clean baseline, Security and the rest)
- Select all and Clear selection
- Load on a named session
- Start fresh
- Reset all in the timeline header, which puts every moved scenario back
- Import setup

Press Undo, or Ctrl+Z (Cmd+Z on a Mac), within ten seconds. Undo puts the form back as it was before that one action. Start fresh reloads the page, and its Undo still works afterwards.

Ctrl+Z does nothing while you are typing in a text field, so it never competes with editing. Only the last action can be undone, and the link goes away after ten seconds. See [[sessions]].

articles.title: Export and import a setup
articles.summary: Save the form to a file, apophis-setup.json, and load it on another copy.
articles.body:
A setup file holds what a named session holds: company, industry, networks, size, ticked scenarios, timing moves, OT options, recipes and whether a campaign is armed. Use it to move a setup to another computer or share one with a colleague.

Under Settings, Sessions, press Export setup to download `apophis-setup.json`. Press Import setup and choose a file to load one.

## What import checks

- A file that is not a setup file, or is too large, is refused with a message.
- A file from a newer version of the app is refused.
- A file with nothing to load is refused.
- Size and minutes moved outside their limits are brought back inside them.
- Names that look like keys, passwords or tokens are ignored, so a setup file never carries a secret.

A refused file changes nothing. An import that works can be undone. See [[undo-a-change]] and [[sessions]].

articles.title: Earlier builds are kept
articles.summary: A rebuild with different settings keeps the earlier build in an earlier-builds folder.
articles.body:
Building again into the same output folder does not destroy the capture that is already there.

- **Different settings.** The earlier capture, its key log, manifest, reports and certificates move to `earlier-builds/<UTC time>-<name>/` inside the output folder, and stay there. The time is when that build was made.
- **Identical settings.** The files are replaced, so you keep one set. Settings include the version, size, date, company, networks, scenarios, timing moves and the content of any recipe or campaign. A new app version counts as a different setting.
- **Stop or failure.** The partial build is removed and the earlier build is put back.

After a build that displaced an earlier one, the result shows "Earlier build kept in" and the folder. Kept builds appear in Captures, under Earlier captures, with a small Kept tag. Open report, Use for replay, Remove and Restore on a kept row act on that kept build's own folder, never on the current capture. The command line prints where the earlier build went.

## Limits

- Only the capture's own files are moved aside: names that start with its name, and the company's threat-collection files. A file named with a custom `--iocs-prefix` is overwritten, not kept.
- Certificates and a key log written outside the output folder, with `--certs-dir` or `--keylog`, are still overwritten.
- If the app stops in the middle of a build, a hidden `.replacing-` folder or a kept folder may be left in the output folder. Nothing is lost; open the folder to find the files.
- Remove moves a capture to the holding folder and does not delete it. See [[captures-and-files]].

articles.title: Starting points, categories and scenario cards
articles.summary: Starting points, categories and cards.
articles.body:
A scenario is network behaviour added on top of the normal day. See [[baseline-and-scale]].

## Starting points

The Starting point panel in Compose has six buttons: Clean baseline, Security, Performance, Crypto posture, OT / ICS day and Incident replay. Each selects a group of scenarios. Pressing a lit button again removes its scenarios, unless another lit group also covers them. Clean baseline clears every ticked scenario and every timing move. Each starting-point button shows an Undo link for ten seconds. See [[undo-a-change]]. OT / ICS day also turns on the OT network.

## Choose scenarios

The category list on the left has these families: Security, Performance, Crypto posture, Incident replays and Custom recipes. Security has Initial access, Credential access, Discovery, Lateral movement, Command and control, Exfiltration, Impact and Multi-stage campaign. Performance has Slow applications, Packet loss and retransmits, DNS and DHCP faults and Capacity. Crypto posture has Weak TLS and Certificate problems.

Search scenarios matches title, id, protocol and category. Family chips narrow the list. Select all and the per-category select and clear buttons change many scenarios at once.

## Scenario cards

Open a card with Details or from the timeline. It shows:

- chips for family, category, OT-only and Fixed size or Grows with size; a Needs verification chip marks a draft description
- Your sensor should show
- the protocols and hosts involved
- When it happens, its place in the 16 hours
- What happens, step by step

Visualize opens a diagram when one exists. See [[incident-replays]] for the sixteen incident replays and which have diagrams. Add to capture or Remove from capture changes your selection.

## The capture day

The Timeline view has one lane per family, a ruler from start to 16 h, and an always-on Normal day lane. Press a marker to open its card. Map lists scenarios by network zone.

articles.title: The incident replays
articles.summary: The 16 incident replays and the Gentlemen ransomware chain: what each shows a sensor, and how much to trust the details.
articles.body:
An incident replay rebuilds the network side of a publicly reported attack. Nothing is exploited and no payload is sent; the traffic only has the shape a sensor would see. The category is Incident replay in Compose.

## The sixteen replays

Nine came earlier: two NetScaler scenarios, BeyondTrust, Metabase, SharePoint, PAN-OS GlobalProtect, vCenter, the WordPress upgrade race and the Linux IP-options flaw. Seven arrived in 5.5.3:

- **ARMORY CASTLE vCenter chain.** An edge appliance is exploited, then an internal appliance writes to the vCenter directory and takes an administrator account. A sensor should show an accepted empty-password LDAP bind, writes from a non-admin host and large uploads to one outside address.
- **Outlook NTLM leak.** Workstations send NTLM authentication to an outside host over SMB, then HTTP. The harvested account is sprayed at the mail portal.
- **FreeSWITCH SIP MESSAGE.** Scanners sweep the SIP port, then SIP MESSAGE requests reach the call server's api handler. The server calls out and places premium-rate calls.
- **OPTIMJACK skimmer.** A third-party script on a retail site changes size, and visitors' browsers contact new outside domains with POSTs.
- **Puppet report RCE.** An outside agent enrols and sends an oversized report. The configuration server then fetches a stager, opens SSH to nodes and sends out a key.
- **OpenSSH SSHole.** A wave of short SSH connections from different clients, then cryptomining over Stratum.
- **Turla Exchange implant.** The mail server replies to task mail by outbound SMTP and ships large archives to a new destination.

## The Gentlemen ransomware chain

The Gentlemen is a Security scenario in the Multi-stage campaign category, not a replay. It runs reconnaissance, Cobalt Strike beacons to its own team server, rclone-style data theft and a mass SMB rewrite with a `.gentlemen` extension and a ransom note. It follows vendor threat reports; there is no CISA advisory.

## How far to trust the details

The replays carry medium confidence, and the Turla one low. CVE numbers and some details come from press and vendor reports and were not all read from primary records such as NVD. For example, the BeyondTrust dates were checked against press and vendor reports (advisory BT26-05). Confirm a number before you quote it. ESET describes the Cereal toolset differently from what is replayed: the mail-borne tasking here follows the older Turla Exchange pattern, as a stand-in a sensor can see.

## Diagrams

Every incident replay, all 16, and the Gentlemen chain open a diagram from Visualize. Each diagram has a Facts and limits note that says what is confirmed and what is not.

articles.title: Indicator cards
articles.summary: What a card says and how to read the traffic badge.
articles.body:
Each row in the indicator table has a card.

- **What it is and what it sends.** The card says what the indicator is, then "Sends:" with the traffic the campaign will make for it.
- **Linked to.** If a tag, note or source names a known malware family or tool, the card adds one sentence about it, such as "Linked to a name (kind)". The 40 families come from a catalog inside the app. Nothing is looked up online.
- **The badge.** "on the wire" means the indicator will put packets in the capture. "no traffic" means it will not. Hover it to read why.
- **Preview traffic.** Shows the actions, protocols and hosts that indicator alone would produce. It comes from the same code that builds the capture, so the two agree.
- **The plan.** Above Compile campaign, a list of the stages the current selection will build.
- **Dropped.** Indicators that could not appear on the wire sit in the Dropped fold with a reason. These are file hashes, file names, e-mail addresses, IPv6 addresses, address ranges and CVEs for products that are not network-facing.

An indicator with no role sends nothing until you give it one.

For CVE cards, see [[cve-profiles-and-exploit-probe]].

articles.title: CVE profiles and the exploit probe
articles.summary: How a CVE becomes an inert attempt against a product class.
