articles.body:
A CVE from the CISA known-exploited list is matched to a product class by its vendor, product and name. The classes are VPN gateway, mail server, file transfer, remote management, web application and network device. When 5.5.0 was measured, 683 of the 1,790 entries could be played as traffic. 5.5.3 recognises more products (Puppet and Perforce as remote management, MONAI and REDCap as web applications, Synology and DiskStation as network devices), so the number is a little higher.

The card shows CISA's own description and required action.

## The exploit probe

The Exploit-attempt probe is a campaign action in the Initial access stage. It does three things.

- An outside host asks for a typical endpoint of the product class.
- It posts a harmless form to two endpoints.
- The server refuses with a 403.

The CVE number travels in a request header so you can trace it. There is no exploit string, shellcode or payload. Every body is filler.

In Build you can change the product class, the CVE, the Host header, the path and whether TLS is used.

## What it does not do

A sensor that watches for exploit content will not fire. The probe tests whether a sensor notices the pattern of an attempt. A CVE whose product is not network-facing, such as a browser, is hidden. See [[indicator-cards]].

articles.title: What pasting a report keeps
articles.summary: Which parts of pasted prose become indicators, and which do not.
articles.body:
When pasted text reads as prose, the builder is careful about what it takes.

## Kept

- IPv4 addresses.
- Defanged hosts, such as `hxxp://example[.]com`. The builder reads them as the real host.

## Left out

- Live links. In a report they are citations, not threats.
- Domains that do not end in a real top-level domain. The builder checks a bundled IANA list. This removes file names and method names that look like domains.
- Government, standards and security-press sites.
- Hashes, file names and CVEs found in the middle of prose. They cannot be played from prose. Paste them as a list, or fetch a feed.

## Lists

If you paste a plain list or a CSV, STIX, MISP, OTX or ThreatFox export, the format is detected. Lines it does not recognise are counted in the status line.

Domains, URLs and hashes stay as written in the capture. Public addresses are moved into a benchmark range. See [[campaign-from-a-threat-report]].

articles.title: Campaign feeds
articles.summary: The 27 feeds, what the info badge says and which need a key.
articles.body:
Under Public feeds there are 27 feeds, plus From a URL for any https list.

**The info badge.** Hover the badge beside a feed. It says which indicator types the feed gives and which of those send traffic. Types that never send traffic by themselves, such as file hashes, file names, e-mail addresses and CVEs for products that are not network-facing, are listed as hidden.

**Keys.** ThreatFox, URLhaus, OTX and Shodan need a key. A key you type stays in the page and goes only to that feed's publisher. You can choose to keep it in the key store. See [[where-keys-are-stored]]. A link you type under From a URL is cached by its host only, with a hash of the full address, so a token in the link is not kept. Shodan has a query box. The default is `has_vuln:true`.

**Offline.** Tick Offline (cache only) to read only what was fetched before.

## What changed

- Removed: MalwareBazaar (hashes only), Feodo Tracker (its lists are empty), the Emerging Threats compromised-host list (no campaign traffic) and Botvrij (not updated since February 2026).
- Added: CINS Army, IPsum, Phishing.Database (addresses and domains), PhishTank, DShield, Spamhaus DROP and Shodan.
- Added later: SiberKapan and Infoblox (MISP feeds), APNIC honeynet (SSH, Telnet and malware URLs) and CERT Polska domains.

## Good to know

- The APNIC Telnet feed lists real Telnet attackers, but the campaign has no Telnet action. Its addresses send SSH or RDP logon attempts instead.
- SiberKapan addresses are treated as scanners. The APNIC malware URLs often point at a bare address and port.
- Spamhaus DROP lists netblocks. One address stands in for each block.

Each feed has its own terms of use. A feed can change its format without notice.

articles.title: Search Help
articles.summary: Find an article by typing what you want to do.
articles.body:
Press the ? icon in the top bar, or press Ctrl or Cmd + K from any screen.

- Type plain words, such as "replay a capture" or "make a pcap". Every word you type has to match.
- The status line says how many results there are. If there are none, try fewer words.
- Titles count most, then keywords, then summaries, then the full text.
- When you open Help from a screen, the articles for that screen come first, under "On this screen".
- Open an article, then use the back button to return to your results. Related articles are at the bottom.

articles.title: Let an AI agent drive the app
articles.summary: Turn on agent access, hand over a token and check what it did.
articles.body:
Use this when you want an AI assistant or a script to build and run scenarios for you. It reaches the app only on this computer.

## Steps

1. Open Settings and find Agent access. Access token says Off.
2. Press Create token. The token is copied to your clipboard and a message says Token copied. Paste it into your agent.
3. Access token now says On. The token is kept in the system keychain, or in a private file beside the settings where there is no keychain.
4. Give the token to your agent client. It sends it as `Authorization: Bearer` with each call. To connect an MCP client, see [[mcp-adapter]].
5. Ask the agent to build a capture. It polls its own build until it finishes. Look in Captures for the result.
6. To see what it did, open `agent-audit.log` in the settings folder. Each call is one line with the time, the verb, the status and the names of the arguments. Values are never written, not even short ones, because a short value can still be a link that carries a key.

## Take access back

- Press Replace token. The old token stops working at once, and a new one is copied.
- Press Turn off. The token is removed and the API goes quiet until you create another.

## If something goes wrong

- The agent gets nothing back. Access token must say On. The API answers only on `127.0.0.1`, so the agent has to run on this computer.
- Replay or a sensor push does not work for the agent. That is by design. See [[agent-limits]].

articles.title: Review a sensor push an agent staged
articles.summary: Check the details and press the push button yourself.
articles.body:
An agent cannot push to a sensor. It can only record a request. You decide.

## Steps

1. Open Settings, Agent access. Staged sensor push shows the sensor and the certificate folder. If nothing is waiting it says None waiting.
2. Press Review. The app switches to Lab, opens Sensor pushes and fills in the sensor, folder, protocol and port.
3. Check the details. A message says Check the details, then press the push button yourself.
4. Press the push button. The key saved for that sensor in Settings is used, as in [[lab-sensor-pushes]].

To refuse a request, press Dismiss instead.

## Good to know

- A staged push expires after 15 minutes.
- The agent sends the sensor address only. A request that carries a key is refused.
- The page checks for a waiting request every 15 seconds.

## If something goes wrong

- Review is grayed out. Nothing is waiting, or the request has expired. Ask the agent to stage it again.
- The push fails. The sensor needs its key saved first. See [[settings-and-lab-switch]].

articles.title: What the agent API is
articles.summary: A local door for AI agents, and when to use it.
articles.body:
The agent API lets an outside assistant drive the app: an AI client, a script or a CI job. It lives at `/agent/v1/` on this computer.

## When to use it

- An AI agent should build and run scenarios for you, such as "build a ransomware campaign and make a capture".
- A script should build the same capture every night.
- You want a record of what a tool did on your behalf.

For work you do yourself, use the app. This is for tools.

## What it can do

It can read what the app can build, read a threat feed or a pasted report, compile and check campaigns, keep a campaign library, run builds as background jobs, list finished captures and check a sensor. See [[agent-verbs]].

## What it cannot do

It cannot replay traffic to a network, and it cannot push to a sensor. Those stay with you. See [[agent-limits]].

## How to start

Create a token in Settings. See [[let-an-agent-drive-the-app]]. The API is off until a token exists.

articles.title: What an agent can ask for
articles.summary: The verbs, grouped by what they do.
articles.body:
An agent calls verbs under `/agent/v1/`. Bodies are the same JSON the app uses. `verbs` lists them.

- **catalog.** Read what the app can build: actions, ATT&CK, templates, feeds, modules and capabilities.
- **intel.** `intel/fetch` reads a threat feed. `intel/parse` reads pasted text.
- **campaign.** Compile, validate, estimate, preview and run a campaign. A campaign that is not valid gets a 400 error with a plain message.
- **library.** List, save, load and import saved campaigns.
- **build.** `build/submit` starts a build. `build/status` shows it. `build/cancel` stops it. A build runs in the background, so an agent submits, then polls until it stops running. `build/submit` takes the same `shifts` option as the app to move scenarios in time; see [[move-scenarios-in-time]].
- **capture.** List finished captures and read a manifest.
- **sensor.** `sensor/check` and `sensor/preflight` are read-only checks. `sensor/stage` records a push for you to review. `sensor/pending` lists what is waiting.

## Sensors

An agent sends the sensor address only. The app uses the key you saved for that sensor in Settings. A request that carries a key is refused.

For campaign terms, see [[build-a-campaign]].

articles.title: What an agent can never do
articles.summary: The limits, and the cookie that scripts now need.
articles.body:
These limits are built in.

- **No replay, push or scoring.** There is no agent verb for any of them. Replay, sensor push and detection scoring stay with a person in the app. An agent can run the read-only sensor check.
- **One door.** A token is refused with a 403 on every route outside `/agent/v1/`.
- **The sensor key stays put.** It never passes through the agent. A staged push is only a request, which you confirm. See [[review-a-staged-sensor-push]].
- **The app's folder only.** `capture/list` ignores any `out_dir` you send and lists the app's own folder. The scale of a campaign run or estimate is capped at the limit the page uses.
- **Local only.** The API answers on `127.0.0.1`.
- **A log.** Every call is written to `agent-audit.log` in the settings folder: time, verb, status and argument names, never a value. The folder is private to you (mode 0700) and the log is readable only by you (0600).

## The cookie change

From 5.5.1, the replay and sensor push routes, and `/api/agent/*`, need the `og_ui` cookie that the app sets when its page loads. From 5.5.5, so do Check sensor and detection scoring, the two routes that can use a stored sensor key. A script that called any of them without the cookie, such as an old curl line for replay, now gets 403. Add the cookie, or do it in the app. The agent verb `sensor/check` is unaffected: it arrives with a token and is written to the audit log.

## What this does not stop

Any program on this computer can read that cookie, and a process that can run programs can start replay tools directly. The check stops agent tools that speak HTTP. It does not stop someone with a shell on the machine.

articles.title: The MCP adapter
articles.summary: Point an MCP client at the app.
articles.body:
`og_mcp.py` is a small adapter that lets an MCP client use the agent API. It speaks over stdio and offers each verb as a tool.

## Set it up

1. Create a token in Settings. See [[let-an-agent-drive-the-app]].
2. In your client's MCP settings, add a server that runs `python3` with `og_mcp.py`.
3. Set the environment variable `OG_AGENT_TOKEN` to your token.

The setting looks like this:

```
{"command": "python3", "args": ["og_mcp.py"], "env": {"OG_AGENT_TOKEN": "<token>"}}
```

The adapter talks to `http://127.0.0.1:8765`. Set `OG_URL` to use another address.

The app must be running, and the token must be on. The same limits apply: no replay, no push. See [[agent-limits]].

articles.title: The question-mark tips
articles.summary: Short notes sit behind the ? icons.
articles.body:
Many screens keep their short explanations behind a ? icon, so the panel stays clear.

- Hover the ? icon, or move to it with the Tab key, to read the note.
- Some icons appear only when there is something to say, such as a note about the capture date or the chosen protocols.
- For longer help, press Ctrl or Cmd + K and search. See [[search-help]].

articles.title: Move a scenario in time
articles.summary: Slide a scenario along the capture day to change when it fires. The traffic itself stays the same.
articles.body:
## What it does

Every scenario has a default window on the capture day. You can slide it earlier or later. Only the timing changes: the same traffic happens, at a different time in the pcap.

## How to move one

- Drag its marker along the timeline. It moves in whole minutes and stops at its limit.
- Or focus a marker and press Alt with the left or right arrow: 1 minute each press. Add Shift for 15 minutes. Bare arrow keys still move between markers.
- Or open the scenario card, type minutes in Move by (negative is earlier), and press Reset to go back to the default. A faint dashed mark shows where a moved scenario started.
- Press Escape while dragging to put everything back.
- Timing: N moved, with a Reset all button, sits in the header of The capture day. It counts every moved scenario, ticked or not, and reads such as "Timing: 3 moved (1 unticked)". A move on an unticked one is kept and returns when you tick it. Reset all, or Clean baseline, clears every move; Undo brings them back.

## Limits

- Everything stays inside the capture day, 05:00 to 21:00. A scenario keeps a margin inside that range, 2 minutes at the start and 5 at the end, and a drag stops at the edge. A value typed or sent past the edge is refused, not trimmed.
- A few scenarios stay near their hours because they only make sense there: the nightly backup, one Volt Typhoon scenario and the three crypto posture scenarios have a narrower range. The card shows the range.
- Some scenarios cannot move: the OT sanctioned writes (tied to the shift changes in the normal day), a custom import, and a campaign. A campaign takes its start time from its own Start option in the campaign editor.
- Some scenarios tell one story and move together: the firewall update with the edge exploit, and the TCP loss storm with Salt Typhoon. Moving one moves the other.

## What to expect

- A moved scenario has the same size and content as before, give or take a few percent. Random details such as sizes and ports differ a little.
- The rest of the day changes only slightly between two different moves. A day with no moves is exactly the day you always got.
- The diagrams, the generation report and the manifest show the moved times. Moves are saved with the session.

## From an agent or script

`build/submit` (and `/api/generate`) accepts `shifts`: an object of scenario name to whole minutes, for example `{"npm-nightly-backup": -30}`. A scenario that is not selected, cannot move or is out of range gets a 400 error with the allowed range. Give a linked scenario the same value as its partner, or leave the partner out and it follows. `catalog/modules` lists each scenario's `start_min` and `end_min` (minutes after 05:00), `shift_limits` and `shift_partner`.
